comments.text: What an extraordinary journey through geologic time! 2 continents collide and form a supercontinent (Rodinia), thrusting up mountains, which then are eroded level – with just the Blue Ridge and Adirondacks remaining.   Then a sea forms (Iapetus), first pulling on the mountains and then  reversing, with its own volcanic islands first colliding and then subducting, thrusting mountains up again. Then the northwest edge of Africa rams into Laurentia during creation of a supercontinent (Pangea), making a mountain chain as high as the Himalayas and longer than any other chain before or since. Unceasing erosion lowers and smooths the mountains, but not before the newly forming Atlantic cuts the long chain into 4 pieces – 4 mountain ranges on 3 continents (Appalachians – North America) (Scottish Highlands + Scandinavian Mountains – Europe) (Anti-Atlas – Africa)! Finally, the smooth rounded Appalachians are uplifted to where they are today. From the 13 original British colonies Euroamericans pour through the Cumberland Gap to settle the lands to the west. This is accompanied by a tragedy, the removal of Native Americans in 1838 by General Winfield Scott – the Trail of Tears. The ridges and valleys created by the formation of Pangea are made sharper by constant unceasing river erosion. This creates dead end hollows, exactly where huge deposits of coal lie. Coal companies rush to fill the demand for energy of the American industrial revolution. Their business practices create an absolute monopoly over every aspect of the lives of the men they recruit to work the coal mines. Their merciless treatment of the now utterly dependent workers leads to strikes, met with violence by the mine owners. The plight of the miners is summarised in the song (Tennessee Ernie Ford) “You load 16 tons, what d’ya get, another day older and deeper in debt. Saint Peter don’t you call me, cos’ I cain’t go, I owe my soul to the company store.“ Having exhausted the veins of coal accessible by tunneling, the mining companies remove the tops of the mountains, insensitively and arrogantly termed ‘overburden.‘  The environment suffers, many forms of wildlife disappear, and occasional heavy storms result in floods and mud slides. The arboral flora is devastated by chestnut blight. (Many of the older generation learned the Longfellow poem by heart which begins ‘Under the spreading chestnut tree, the village smithy stands…‘ )  Thank you for this fascinating explanation of the complex formation of the Appalachians, showing us that what one sees and thinks one knows is but a momentary snapshot during eons of geologic processes that are still going on
